title: Scaling Laws for Mixture Pretraining Under Data Constraints
gist: Across more than 2,000 language-model training runs, Apple researchers find that mixing scarce target-domain data with abundant generic data tolerates far higher repetition than single-source training (scarce corpora can be reused 15-20 times), and they introduce a repetition-aware mixture scaling law that yields principled, computable mixture recommendations for pretraining under data constraints.

insights.claim: When mixing scarce target-domain data with abundant generic data during pretraining, too little target data underexposes the model to the target domain while too much target data causes excessive repetition, diminishing returns, and eventual overfitting, creating a fundamental trade-off in mixture design.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Any team pretraining models on low-resource languages, specialized domains, or proprietary datasets faces a real optimization problem in mixture ratio, not just an intuition call, and getting it wrong costs compute either way (underexposure or overfitting).
insights.quote: too little target data in the mixture underexposes the model to the target domain, while too much target data repeats the same examples excessively, yielding diminishing returns and eventual overfitting
insights.locator: Scaling Laws for Mixture Pretraining Under Data Constraints abstract

themes.theme: Repetition tolerance is much higher in mixture training

insights.claim: Across more than 2,000 language-model training runs spanning multiple model sizes, target dataset sizes, and data types (multilingual, domain-specific, quality-filtered), repetition is a central driver of target-domain performance, and mixture training tolerates far higher repetition of the scarce data than single-source training does.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Teams with limited target-domain data have been under-utilizing it if they assumed low repetition limits from single-source-training folklore; mixing with generic data materially raises the safe reuse ceiling and can improve final model quality.
insights.quote: we find that repetition is a central driver of target-domain performance, and that mixture training tolerates much higher repetition than single-source training
insights.locator: Scaling Laws for Mixture Pretraining Under Data Constraints abstract

insights.claim: Scarce target-domain corpora can be reused 15-20 times within a data mixture without the overfitting penalty seen in single-source training, with the exact optimal repetition count depending on target data size, compute budget, and model scale.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A concrete 15-20x reuse figure gives practitioners an actionable starting point for how aggressively to epoch over scarce target data before diminishing returns set in, rather than relying on guesswork.
insights.quote: scarce target corpora can be reused 15–20 times, with the optimal number of repetitions depending on the target data size, compute budget, and model scale
insights.locator: Scaling Laws for Mixture Pretraining Under Data Constraints abstract

themes.theme: A repetition-aware scaling law for mixture design

insights.claim: The researchers introduce a repetition-aware mixture scaling law that accounts for the decreasing marginal value of repeated target tokens and the regularizing role generic data plays, and optimizing this law provides a principled method to compute effective mixture configurations rather than relying on trial and error.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A closed-form, computable scaling law for mixture ratios lets labs skip expensive trial-and-error sweeps when designing pretraining data mixtures, directly reducing compute cost for any team training on constrained target data.
insights.quote: we introduce a repetition-aware mixture scaling law that accounts for the decreasing value of repeated target tokens and the regularizing role of generic data
insights.locator: Scaling Laws for Mixture Pretraining Under Data Constraints abstract
